title: Threats Against the AI Model and Data

blocks.text: Objective 2.6 is **new in version 8** and none of the four provided books covers it. All concepts in this lesson come from the **official §2.6 objectives** and are marked "Outside books".
The books mention AI/ML only as a **defensive tool** (behavioral detection, UEBA, EDR — SOC Notes pp. 109, 196; 11 Strategies pp. 193, 264). They describe no threats related to the use of AI.

blocks.note: Official list of 13 concepts — no source book

blocks.field: Unauthorized modification of a model's behavior or parameters to make it act differently than intended.
Injecting malicious data into training data to bias or weaken the learned model.
Crafting adversarial inputs designed to bypass the model's detection or classification.

blocks.text: Key difference: **poisoning** acts **upstream**, during training; **evasion** acts **downstream**, at inference time; **manipulation** targets the model or its parameters directly.
Data as Both Target and Risk

blocks.field: Disclosure or loss of confidential information via an AI system: sensitive data entered into a public tool, memorized by the model, or exposed in logs.
Risk that personal data is collected, retained, or output without legal basis or user control.

blocks.q: An attacker injects mislabeled examples into the training dataset. Which threat is this?
blocks.explain: Poisoning acts on training data, hence upstream. Evasion acts on inputs at inference time.

items: Model manipulation = unauthorized change in behavior.
Data loss and privacy concern data entrusted to the AI system.

title: Threats Related to AI Usage and Output

blocks.text: The second family targets interaction with the model: what it is asked, what it bypasses, and what it produces.

blocks.field: Malicious instructions hidden in an input (document, message, web page) that hijack the model away from its initial instruction.
Technique aimed at making the model ignore its safety restrictions to obtain normally refused content.

left.title: Prompt Injection
points: The attack arrives **via the content** processed by the model.
Example: a PDF containing "ignore previous instructions".
Aims to hijack the requested task.

right.title: Jailbreaking
points: The attack targets **the model's safety rules**.
Example: fictional roleplay, encoding, disguised requests.

blocks.text: A hostile instruction hidden in an analyzed document = **prompt injection**. A series of prompts to bypass rules = **jailbreaking**. Both can be combined.

blocks.field: The model produces a fluent but factually false or fabricated response, with misleading confidence.
Systematic bias in data or the model, producing discriminatory or skewed results.
Ability to understand and justify why a model produced a given output — critical in security and compliance.
Responsible use, fairness, transparency, accountability for errors, and societal impact of AI systems.
Theft or reuse of a user's or AI agent's session to act with their privileges.
An AI agent with tool access can be tricked into executing unauthorized commands or code on the host environment.

blocks.text: An AI agent with access to tools (shell, API, database) must be treated as a **privileged account**: least privilege, logging, guardrails, and reversibility.

blocks.note: All 13 concepts are officially on the exam; none in the books

blocks.q: A corporate chatbot outputs to another customer an excerpt from a confidential contract entered earlier. Which concept is most directly involved?
blocks.explain: Leaking confidential data through the AI system is data loss and a privacy issue.

items: Prompt injection = hostile content; jailbreaking = bypassing rules.
Hallucination = false but credible; bias = systematically skewed result.
AI agent = privileged identity to control (session, code execution).
